pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 5–7 (Year 1 → Year 2). SKIP COUNTING in 2s, 5s and 10s — the first move beyond counting by ones into counting equal GROUPS. The gateway to multiplication (equal groups / repeated addition), even numbers, telling time (5s) and place value (10s).
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 1 'count in multiples of 2s, 5s and 10s'; guidance: 'counting in 2s, 5s and 10s from different multiples to develop their recognition of patterns in the number system (for example, odd and even numbers).'
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.1 'count … by tens'; Grade 2 extends — 2.NBT.2 'Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s.' Skip counting underpins the multiplication foundations of 2.OA.3–4 and Grade 3 OA.
• Operational details: Teach as counting equal GROUPS, not a new chant — each 'step' is one more group of 2/5/10 (link to repeated addition, the multiplication seed). Use the HUNDRED SQUARE (shade 5s → two columns; 10s → one column; 2s → even columns) and the NUMBER LINE (equal jumps landing on multiples) so the pattern is seen. Count from different starting multiples, not only 0. Anchor 2s↔even, 5s↔clock/tallies/fingers, 10s↔place value.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5–6) counts in 10s to 100 and 2s to 20 from 0. Tier B (6) counts in 5s to 50 and links 2s to even numbers. Tier C (6–7) counts in 2s/5s/10s from a non-zero multiple and explains each step adds a group ('5s go up by five each time = one more group of five').
bestPractices: Teach each skip count as adding one equal GROUP (repeated addition), not a disconnected chant — this is the multiplication seed.
Shade multiples on a hundred square so the visual pattern (columns/diagonals) makes the sequence predictable rather than memorised.
Use a number line with equal-sized jumps landing on multiples — the jump size IS the step, making 'counting in 5s' concrete.
Count from different starting multiples and in both directions so it is flexible, not a fixed rote song.
Anchor to real contexts: 2s (pairs, even numbers), 5s (fingers, tally marks, clock minutes), 10s (tens, money).
keyRepresentations: Hundred square with multiples shaded (pattern by column/diagonal).
Number line with equal jumps (the jump = the step size).
Equal groups / arrays of 2, 5, 10 (the bridge to multiplication).
commonMisconceptions: Reciting the multiples as a chant with no sense that each step is +one group — so it doesn't transfer to multiplication.
Thinking the multiples are the ONLY numbers that 'exist', or that skip counting removes the in-between numbers (7 isn't 'skipped away').
Only able to start from 0 — can't skip-count from a different multiple or backwards.
Confusing 'counting in 2s' with 'counting to 2', or losing the pattern at decade boundaries (5s: '…45, 50, 55').

learn.summary: Skip counting in 2s, 5s and 10s for ages 5–7, taught as counting equal GROUPS (one more group of 2/5/10 each step) rather than a memorised chant — the bridge to multiplication, repeated addition, even numbers, clock minutes and place value. Core representations are the hundred square (on a standard 10-wide square, shaded multiples of 2, 5 and 10 form straight column patterns) and the number line (equal-sized jumps landing on multiples). Learners should count from different starting multiples and in both directions, not only forward from 0.

activities.title: One hop, one group: linking jumps, counters and the hundred square
feedback: If a learner recites fluently from 0 but can't say what comes after 40 in 10s, bring them back to one jump: 'each hop adds ten — show me the next group.'
When the shaded 10s form a single straight column and the 5s two columns, prompt: 'what do you notice about where they are?' so the pattern, not memory, drives the next number.

If a learner sub-counts the in-between numbers under their breath, that is a normal developing step — let the equal jump and the shaded pattern gradually make it feel like one move; do not mark it wrong.
If starting at 30 they restart from 0, say 'start here and keep hopping' and practise entering mid-sequence from several multiples.
activities.rationale: Showing the jump, the stacked group of counters and the shaded hundred-square cells together makes 'counting in fives' concrete as repeated equal groups rather than a chant, and counting from varied multiples and in both directions keeps it flexible. Linked, simultaneously-moving views (number line + counters + hundred square) are offered as one way to make the group structure visible; the panels moving together is an optional interaction example, not a required mechanism.
sourceClaims: Year 1: 'count in multiples of 2s, 5s and 10s'; guidance: counting in 2s, 5s and 10s from different multiples to develop recognition of number patterns (e.g. odd and even).
2.NBT.2 'Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s'; skip counting underpins multiplication foundations (equal groups / repeated addition).
Skip counting is taught as counting equal groups (the multiplication bridge) using the hundred square and number line to make patterns visible.
learnerActions: Pick which step size you are counting in: 2, 5 or 10.
Take one step forward on a number line, making an equal-sized jump (a jump of 5 for 5s) that lands on the next multiple.
For each jump, add a GROUP of that many counters into a new stack/tower, so you see the jump as 'one more group of five'.
Shade or light up the cells you land on (5, 10, 15 …) on a hundred square as you go.
Say aloud what each step adds: 'each hop adds five — one more group of five.'
Try starting from a non-zero multiple (e.g. start at 30 and count on in 10s: 30, 40, 50 …).
Try counting in the other direction too (e.g. count back in 10s from 50: 50, 40, 30 …).
activities.intendedInsight: Each step of skip counting adds (or, going back, removes) one equal group, so the next multiple can be predicted from the pattern and from 'one more group' instead of recited — this is the seed of multiplication and repeated addition.

activities.title: Spotting the pattern on a multiples chart
feedback: If a learner says the multiples are the 'only numbers that exist' or that in-between numbers are 'skipped away', point to the chart: 7 is still there, we are just landing on every second/fifth/tenth number.
At a decade boundary, if they lose the pattern (…45, 50, 55), have them trace the column to confirm the next landing cell.
activities.rationale: A pre-marked multiples chart is a genuinely useful reference whose pattern is visible even when static; it supports recognising multiples and crossing decade boundaries. It shows the pattern but does not itself require the learner to generate each step, so pair it with tasks where the learner constructs and explains steps.
sourceClaims: Year 1: 'count in multiples of 2s, 5s and 10s'; guidance: counting in 2s, 5s and 10s from different multiples to develop recognition of number patterns (e.g. odd and even).
learnerActions: Look at a hundred square or multiples chart with the 2s, 5s or 10s already marked.
Tap or point to a multiple to reveal it and the group it stands for (e.g. 15 = three groups of five).
Describe the visual pattern: 10s make one straight column, 5s make two columns, 2s shade the even columns.
Use the chart as a reference to answer 'what comes next in 5s after 45?' across a decade boundary.
activities.intendedInsight: The multiples sit in a predictable visual pattern, so you can find the next one by reading the pattern rather than restarting the chant — and the pattern survives decade boundaries like 45, 50, 55.

activities.title: Anchoring 2s, 5s and 10s to real things
feedback: If a learner confuses 'counting in 2s' with 'counting to 2', re-ground in pairs: each new pair adds two to the total.
Use fingers and tally marks to re-establish the fives if the 5s pattern slips.
activities.rationale: Anchoring each step size to familiar contexts gives meaning to the groups and supports transfer to even numbers, telling time and place value.
sourceClaims: Year 1: 'count in multiples of 2s, 5s and 10s'; guidance: counting in 2s, 5s and 10s from different multiples to develop recognition of number patterns (e.g. odd and even).
learnerActions: Count pairs of objects in 2s and connect to even numbers (2, 4, 6 …).
Count hands/fingers and tally marks in 5s (5, 10, 15 …) and clock minutes in 5s.
Count groups of ten — tens blocks or 10p coins — in 10s and link to place value (how many tens).
Say how each context shows 'one more group': one more pair, one more hand of five, one more ten.
activities.intendedInsight: Skip counting describes real repeated groups — pairs, fives and tens — so 2s↔even, 5s↔clock/tallies/fingers, 10s↔place value make the counts meaningful and memorable.

activities.title: Fluency practice: fill, continue, match
feedback: A 'next multiple' or 'fill the gap' task checks fluency but, on its own, may let a learner answer by recognition; follow up with 'how did you know?' to check for group reasoning.
In the oral partner game, use the caught slip to prompt 'how did you know that was wrong?' rather than just correcting.
activities.rationale: These tasks give targeted fluency practice and the array-matching links sequences back to equal groups. Fill/continue tasks check recall and recognition but do not by themselves show the learner is reasoning from groups, so pair them with the construction and explanation tasks. The oral call-and-response gives fluency and listening practice but lacks a seen pattern, so it complements rather than replaces the visual work.
learnerActions: Fill in a missing multiple in a sequence (…, 10, __, 20 in 5s).
Say what comes next in 2s/5s/10s from a given number, including across a decade boundary.
Put a set of multiples in order.
Match a skip-count (e.g. 5, 10, 15) to an array or picture of equal groups.
Do an oral count-in-5s with a partner as call-and-response, and catch a deliberate slip in the other person's count.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated varied practice — including continuing from non-zero starts and matching counts to equal-group arrays — builds fluency while keeping the count tied to groups.

constraints: Teach skip counting as adding one equal group each step (repeated addition), not as a disconnected chant — this is the multiplication seed.
Count from different starting multiples (not only 0) and in both directions, so the skill is flexible rather than a fixed rote song.

A pre-marked multiples chart and fill/continue practice items are references and recognition checks; they show or test the pattern but do not require the learner to independently construct each step, so pair them with tasks where the learner generates and explains steps.

Reverting to counting the in-between numbers by ones, and difficulty starting from a non-zero multiple, are developmental stages that improve with practice — do not mark them as errors; scaffold with equal jumps and hundred-square patterns.
Do not imply that only the multiples 'exist' or that in-between numbers are removed; the full number sequence is still present, we just land on every 2nd/5th/10th number.
Watch decade boundaries in 5s (…45, 50, 55) where the pattern is easily lost.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels the CCSS 2.NBT.2 and NCETM claims as verified:false; only the DfE Year 1 claim is marked verified. Treat the standards-alignment and 'taught as equal groups' statements as unverified; they are retained only where they directly support the equal-groups principle.

The legacy note that a third dimension 'adds nothing' to a grid/line pattern was removed as a catalog-fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law; a planar hundred square and number line are well-suited here, which is sufficient without the universal claim.

The legacy framing of one interactive as 'the killer move' / 'the insight clicks' was softened: the linked number-line/counters/hundred-square views are presented as one effective way to make equal groups visible, not as uniquely necessary.

The oral call-and-response and static chart are described by narrow affordances (fluency/listening practice; visible but non-generative reference); no categorical 'only this teaches' or 'cannot teach' claim is asserted.
Catalog/product vocabulary ('quiz', artefact-fit rankings) was removed from learner-facing text; where mentioned in these notes it only documents the removal.

probeDeeper: What comes after 16 when counting in 2s?
Look at the 5s you tapped — what do you notice about where they are?
How is counting in 2s like counting groups of 2?
assess.correctAnswer: Recites 2s, 5s, 10s accurately to the stated limits; the hundred-square taps fall in a straight column (10s) and a regular pattern (5s, 2s); continues 30, 40, 50… when started at 30 — treating skip counting as counting equal groups, not a fixed jingle.

errorPatterns.pattern: skip-counting-as-chant — recites the sequence as a memorised rhyme but can't say what comes after a given multiple without restarting, and can't map it to the numbers
errorPatterns.nextMove: link each step to a group — a jump of 2 on the number line, a column of 10 on the square — saying 'each hop adds two' so the sequence carries meaning
errorPatterns.revealedBy: fluent from 0 yet stuck on 'what's after 40 in 10s?' or unable to point the sequence out on the hundred square

errorPatterns.pattern: reverts to counting by ones — gets the next multiple by counting the ones in between under their breath rather than stepping by the group size
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT treat as an error — the group-step speeds up with practice; use number-line equal jumps and hundred-square patterns to make the step feel like one move

errorPatterns.pattern: can't start from a non-zero multiple — counts in 10s only from 0; asked to start at 30, restarts at 0 or 10
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT correct as a mistake — practise 'start here and keep hopping' from various multiples on a number line; entering mid-sequence develops with exposure

responseLevels.gap: Cannot sustain a skip-count sequence, or produces it only as a memorised chant with no link to the numbers on a track or square.
responseLevels.full: Skip-counts 2s, 5s, 10s to the limits, continues from any multiple, and connects each step to adding an equal group (jumps on a number line, patterns on a hundred square).
responseLevels.partial: Recites 2s/5s/10s from 0 fluently but reverts to counting by ones for the next multiple, or can't start from a non-zero multiple — the equal-group structure isn't yet seen.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Count out loud in 2s from 0 up to 20. Now count in 10s up to 100. Now count in 5s up to 50, and this time point to each number as you say it on this hundred square. Then start at 30 and count on in 10s. (Watch fluency, whether the taps land in the right pattern, and whether they can start from a non-zero multiple.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reciting from 0 is the baseline; the pointing-on-the-square and start-at-30 tasks reveal whether the child sees skip counting as adding equal groups or is just chanting. A chant-only child can say '5,10,15,20' but can't point to them correctly, can't start from 30, or drops back to counting by ones to get the next number.
